mainTopic: Using another's slave or ship without permission, and a stolen coin that cracked or was cancelled.
overview: The גמרא asks how רב can say a slave is like land when he also rules that someone who makes another person's slave work is פטור. It answers that the case is outside working hours, and that the owner even benefits because his slave stays used to working, just as a lived-in courtyard stays in good shape. A story follows: רב יוסף בר חמא used his debtors' slaves. His son רבה shows that for a lender this looks like רבית, and the father takes it back. Next, רב and שמואל argue about someone who uses another's ship, and רב פפא gives two ways to show they do not really disagree. The גמרא then explains the משנה's 'cracked' and 'invalidated' coin. רב הונא and רב יהודה each defend their view, one against rotten fruit and sour wine, the other against impure תרומה. Finally, a new dispute begins about a loan in a coin that was later cancelled, and it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Did רב really say a slave is like land?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב's view that a slave is like real estate, using רב's own ruling that one who forces another's slave to work is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רב really say a slave is like land? But רב דניאל בר רב קטינא said in רב's name: if someone grabs another person's slave and makes him work, he is פטור. If a slave is like land, why is he פטור? The slave is still in his master's possession!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions רב's earlier statement that a slave is like real estate. It points to another ruling of רב that seems to contradict it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Land can never be stolen. It always stays in its owner's possession. So if a slave is like land, the one who seized him never became a גזלן and cannot claim he owns the slave. He simply used someone else's property and should have to pay for the work. רב's ruling of פטור seems to clash with that.

keyTerms.meaning: A slave is like real estate
One who seizes, grabs by force
And if it enters your mind
He stands in his master's possession

steps.confusionAlert: Being פטור here is not because the slave was stolen. The whole point is that, like land, the slave was never stolen. That is exactly why paying for the work seems like it should be required.

phrases.english: And did Rav really say
that a slave is like real estate?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָאָמַר רַב דָּנִיאֵל בַּר רַב קַטִּינָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: But doesn't Rav Daniel bar Rav Ketina say that Rav says:
One who seizes another person's slave
and makes him do work is exempt.
And if it enters your mind
that a slave is like real estate,
why is he exempt?
The slave stands in his master's possession!
phrases.notes: Like land, the slave can't really be stolen. So the grabber just used the owner's property and should pay.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר רַב עַבְדָּא כִּמְקַרְקְעֵי דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's earlier statement in the sugya.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's position that a slave is like real estate.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the slave always stays in the owner's possession, the one who used him took the owner's property and should pay for the labor. Yet רב rules he is פטור.

steps.title: The case is outside working hours
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב's case of פטור is when the slave was used at a time he would not have worked for his master anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with? When the slave was made to work outside of normal working hours.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב by narrowing the case. The slave was used at a time when he was not supposed to be working for his master.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the master was not losing any work at that time, he suffered no loss. The user only gained a benefit without causing a loss, so he does not have to pay. A slave can still be like land.

keyTerms.meaning: With what case are we dealing here?

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here?
With a case not during working hours.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 1.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב's ruling of פטור applies even when the owner lost the slave's work.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ruling is only when the slave was used outside working hours, so the owner lost nothing.

steps.title: Support from living in someone's courtyard
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא compares this to רב הונא's ruling that someone who lives in another's courtyard without permission does not have to pay rent.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like what רבי אבא sent to מרי בר מר: ask רב הונא whether someone who lives in his friend's courtyard without his knowledge must pay him rent. They answered that he does not need to pay rent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a parallel case to support the answer. Using someone's property without causing him any loss does not require payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The courtyard owner was not renting it out anyway, so he lost nothing, even though the resident benefited. The same idea is applied to the slave used outside working hours. Benefit without loss means no payment.

keyTerms.meaning: One who lives in his friend's courtyard

phrases.english: This is like that which was sent
by Rabbi Abba to Mari bar Mar,
Ask Rav Huna:
one who lives in his friend's courtyard without his knowledge,
does he need to pay him rent

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ אֵין צָרִיךְ לְהַעֲלוֹת לוֹ שָׂכָר?
phrases.english: or does he not need to pay him rent?
And they sent to him:
He does not need to pay him rent.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דִּשְׁלַח לֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא לְמָרֵי בַּר מָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 2 with a parallel case.
steps.raayaObject: That using someone's property without causing loss requires no payment.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב הונא's ruling about living in another's courtyard without permission.

steps.title: The courtyard and the slave are not the same
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison. A courtyard owner benefits when someone lives there, but a slave owner doesn't seem to benefit when his slave gets worn out.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare them? There, either way it is good for the owner. One view says a lived-in house stays in good shape, and another learns from 'and the gate is smitten unto ruin' that an empty house falls apart. But here, is the owner happy that his slave gets worn out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the comparison from the courtyard. In the courtyard case the owner actually gains, but in the slave case the owner seems to lose because his slave gets tired.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the courtyard, both explanations agree that someone living there helps the house. In the slave case, extra work weakens the slave, which is a real loss to the owner. So the 'no loss' reasoning seems not to carry over.

keyTerms.meaning: It is good for him, he is pleased

phrases.english: How can these be compared?!
Granted, there, in the courtyard case,
whether according to the one who says
a house that is lived in stays in good shape,
it is good for him,
or according to the one who says
"and the gate is smitten unto ruin"
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 24:12. An empty house falls apart, so having someone live there protects it.

phrases.english: it is good for him.
But here, with the slave,
is it good for him
that his slave gets worn out?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי הַשְׁתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the comparison brought in step 3.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The comparison between the courtyard and the slave, not the answer of step 2 itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The courtyard owner gains from the use, while the slave owner seems to lose because his slave becomes weakened.

steps.title: The owner benefits, since his slave stays used to working
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the slave owner does benefit, because extra work keeps his slave from losing his working habits.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: Indeed, it is good for him, because then his slave doesn't fall out of the habit of working.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the rejection and keeps the comparison. The owner benefits from his slave staying active and used to work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as living in a house keeps it in good shape, working keeps a slave in working condition. An idle slave gets lazy and out of practice. So, just like the courtyard owner, the slave owner gains and suffers no loss.

keyTerms.meaning: Be undone, fall out of practice

steps.whatToRemember: רב can hold a slave is like land and still say one who uses another's slave is פטור. That is only outside working hours, when the owner loses nothing and even benefits, just like living in someone's courtyard.

phrases.english: They say:
Indeed so,
it is good for him
that his slave not lose his working habits.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: הָכִי נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the rejection of step 4 and restores the comparison.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Extra work only harms the owner by wearing out his slave.
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner benefits because his slave stays in the habit of working, so the courtyard comparison holds.

steps.title: רבה asks his father why he uses his debtors' slaves
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף בר חמא would seize the slaves of people who owed him money and make them work. His son רבה asks him why he does this.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף בר חמא used to grab the slaves of people who owed him money and make them work for him. His son רבה asked him: Why does the Master do this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a story about a real-life case that connects to the slave rulings we just learned. רבה's question sets up a back-and-forth with his father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first glance, using someone else's slave without permission seems to mean you owe the owner for the work. Here there is an extra twist: the owners are people who owe רב יוסף בר חמא money. רבה wants to know what allows his father to do this.

keyTerms.meaning: grabs or seizes (takes by force, without permission)
he is owed money by them (they are his debtors)
Master, a respectful way of saying 'you'

phrases.aramaic: (בֵּי) רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר חָמָא הֲווֹ[ה] תָּקֵיף
phrases.english: Rav Yosef bar Chama would seize
phrases.notes: Some versions say 'the household of' רב יוסף בר חמא did this. The corrected wording leaves out the word in round brackets, so he did it himself.

phrases.english: the slaves of people who owed him money,
and he would make them do work.
Rabba his son said to him:
What is the reason the Master does this?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא עָבֵיד מָר הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a real-life story that tests the slave rulings from the earlier steps.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the legal basis for using debtors' slaves without paying?

steps.title: A slave's work is not worth his food
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף בר חמא answers with רב נחמן's rule: a slave is not even worth the food he eats.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Because רב נחמן said: A slave is not worth even the bread in his stomach.
steps.whatsHappening: The father gives his first reason. Using these slaves causes the owners no loss, because the slaves eat more than their work is worth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that he feeds the slaves while they work for him. If their work is worth less than their food, the owner actually comes out ahead. So he owes nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: the bread of his stomach (the food he eats)

phrases.english: He said to him: Because Rav Nachman said:
A slave is not worth the bread of his stomach.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבה's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Slaves' work is worth less than their food, so the owners lose nothing.

steps.title: רבה says that rule is only about a useless slave
steps.stepSummary: רבה pushes back. רב נחמן was talking about his own slave דארו, who only dances among the barrels. Normal slaves do real work.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I would say רב נחמן said that about someone like דארו, his slave, who dances among the barrels. All other slaves do real work!
steps.whatsHappening: רבה rejects his father's first reason by limiting רב נחמן's rule to one special slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן's rule was not a general rule about all slaves. It described a lazy slave like דארו. Real working slaves are worth more than their food, so the owners do lose out.

keyTerms.meaning: I would say (offering a different reading)
the name of רב נחמן's slave

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֵימָא דְּאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
phrases.english: He said to him: I would say that Rav Nachman said this
about someone like Daru, his slave,
who dances among the barrels;
phrases.notes: דארו just fooled around and didn't do real work.

phrases.english: all other slaves do work!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer of step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Limits רב נחמן's rule to a lazy slave, not working slaves.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The rule was taken as general when it only describes a slave who does no work.

steps.title: The father relies on רב's ruling that the user is פטור
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף בר חמא now relies on רב's ruling, said through רב דניאל, that one who uses another's slave is פטור, because the owner is happy his slave keeps working.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I hold like רב דניאל, as רב דניאל בר רב קטינא said in the name of רב: One who seizes another's slave and makes him work is exempt. This shows the owner is pleased that his slave doesn't lose his working habits.
steps.whatsHappening: The father gives a second, stronger reason. It is the same ruling of רב we saw at the start, explained the way the גמרא explained it in step 5.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the reason is not that the slave is worthless. The owner actually gains when his slave keeps busy and stays in the habit of working. So the one who uses the slave owes him nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: exempt, does not have to pay

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֲנָא כְּרַב דָּנִיאֵל סְבִירָא לִי –
phrases.english: He said to him: I hold like Rav Daniel,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב דָּנִיאֵל בַּר רַב קַטִּינָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: as Rav Daniel bar Rav Ketina said in the name of Rav:
One who seizes another's slave
and makes him work is exempt.
phrases.notes: This is the same ruling of רב from step 1.

phrases.english: This shows that it pleases him,
that his slave not lose his working habits.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲנָא כְּרַב דָּנִיאֵל סְבִירָא לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 8 knocked out his first reason, the father brings a new source.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Switches to a different source that does not depend on the slave being worthless.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The father needed the slave's work to be worthless to justify using him.
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner benefits from his slave staying busy, so the user is פטור.

steps.title: With a borrower's slave, it looks like interest
steps.stepSummary: רבה says רב's ruling only works when you are not owed money. If the slave's owner owes you money, the free work looks like רבית.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: That rule applies where he is not owed money by them. But you, Master, since you are owed money by them, it looks like interest.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה accepts רב's ruling but shows it does not fit his father's case. This is because of a new problem: רבית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, using a slave for free is fine because the owner benefits. But when the owner is your borrower, any free benefit you get from him looks like a payment for the loan. That is מחזי כרבית, something that looks like interest.

keyTerms.meaning: these words apply (only in this case)

phrases.english: He said to him: These words apply
where he is not owed money by them;
but you, Master, since you are owed money by them,
it looks like interest.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּלָא מַסֵּיק בְּהוּ זוּזֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the father's use of רב's ruling in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The father's reliance on רב's exemption for using another's slave.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The exemption holds only between strangers. Between a lender and a borrower, free benefit looks like רבית.
steps.confusionAlert: רבה is not arguing with רב's ruling. He agrees the user is פטור in a normal case. He is only saying a lender is different because of רבית.

steps.title: Proof from living in a borrower's courtyard
steps.stepSummary: רבה proves his point from רב נחמן. Normally one who lives in another's courtyard without permission pays no rent, but a lender who does so must pay rent.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב יוסף בר מניומי said in the name of רב נחמן: Even though they said that one who lives in another's courtyard without his knowledge does not need to pay him rent, if he lent him money and then lived in his courtyard, he does need to pay him rent!
steps.whatsHappening: רבה backs up his challenge with a clear parallel case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The courtyard rule is just like the slave rule: normally you owe nothing. Yet רב נחמן says a lender must pay rent so it won't look like רבית. The same must be true when a lender uses his borrower's slave.

keyTerms.meaning: one who lives in another's courtyard

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן,
phrases.english: As Rav Yosef bar Minyumi said in the name of Rav Nachman:
Even though they said:
One who lives in another's courtyard without his knowledge
does not need to pay him rent,
phrases.notes: This is רב הונא's ruling from step 3.

phrases.english: if he lent him money and lived in the other's courtyard,
he does need to pay him rent!

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף בַּר מִנְיוֹמֵי אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the challenge of step 10.
steps.raayaObject: A lender must pay for benefit he takes from his borrower, even where others would be פטור.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב נחמן's ruling that a lender who lives in his borrower's courtyard must pay rent.

steps.title: רב יוסף בר חמא takes it back
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף בר חמא accepts his son's argument and retracts.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I take it back.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with the father agreeing with רבה and stopping his practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This settles the story. A lender may not use his borrower's slave for free, even though a stranger could, because it looks like רבית.
steps.whatToRemember: Using another's slave without permission is normally פטור, because the owner benefits when his slave keeps working. But a lender may not do this to his borrower, because it looks like רבית. The same is true of living in a borrower's courtyard.

phrases.english: He said to him: I take it back.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲדַרִי בִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the challenge and proof of steps 10 and 11.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A lender must not take free work from his borrower's slave, since it looks like רבית.

steps.title: Using someone's ship: rent or damage?
steps.stepSummary: A new case: someone used another person's ship without permission. רב says the owner may choose to collect rent or damage. שמואל says he collects only the damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: One who seizes another's ship and does work with it — רב said: If the owner wants, he takes its rent; if he wants, he takes its damage. And שמואל said: He takes only its damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a מחלוקת between רב and שמואל about using another's ship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is what the ship's owner can collect. רב lets him pick, so he will take whichever is more. שמואל says he can only collect the loss in the ship's value from the use, not rent.

keyTerms.meaning: it was stated (introduces an argument between אמוראים)
its rent (what renting it would cost)
its loss in value (damage from use)

phrases.english: It was stated:
One who seizes another's ship
and does work with it,
Rav said: If he wants, he takes its rent,
if he wants, he takes its damage.
phrases.notes: 'Damage' means how much the ship's value went down from being used.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said:
He takes only its damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר: הַתּוֹקֵף סְפִינָתוֹ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from seizing slaves to a related case of seizing a ship.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: the owner may choose rent or damage. שמואל: he collects only damage.
steps.whyThisMatters: This מחלוקת sets up the next discussion about what a person owes when he uses another's property without permission.

steps.title: No real dispute: it depends on whether the ship is usually rented out
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says רב and שמואל do not argue. רב speaks about a ship that is usually rented out, and שמואל speaks about one that is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: They do not disagree. רב is talking about a ship that people usually rent out. שמואל is talking about a ship that is not usually rented out.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא settles the argument from Step 13 by saying רב and שמואל are each talking about a different kind of ship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner normally earns rent from his ship, the user took away real income, so the owner can ask for rent (רב). If the ship is not normally rented, the owner lost no rent, so he collects only the damage (שמואל).

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: They do not disagree;
this is where it is usually rented out,
phrases.notes: 'This' is רב's ruling, where the owner may choose rent.

phrases.english: that is where it is not usually rented out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the רב–שמואל dispute about the ship by placing each opinion in a different case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each opinion fits a different situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב and שמואל seemed to argue about the very same case of using a ship.
steps.terutzMaskana: A ship usually rented out: the owner may collect rent. A ship not usually rented out: he collects only the damage.

steps.title: Second answer: it depends on the user's intention
steps.stepSummary: Another way to settle the dispute: both opinions speak about a ship that is usually rented out. רב is talking about someone who meant to pay rent, and שמואל is talking about someone who meant to rob.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: both are talking about a ship that is usually rented out. רב is talking about someone who boarded it planning to pay rent. שמואל is talking about someone who boarded it planning to steal its use.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different way to show that רב and שמואל do not really argue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the difference is not the kind of ship but the person's plan. Someone who took it as a renter pays rent. Someone who took it as a robber is treated as a גזלן and pays only for the damage.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces a second answer)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to settle רב and שמואל: (1) is the ship usually rented out or not, or (2) did the user plan to rent it or to rob it.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
both this and that are where it is usually rented out;
this is where he went down into it intending to pay rent,
phrases.notes: 'Went down into it' means he boarded and took the ship. 'This' is רב's ruling.

phrases.english: and that is where he went down into it intending to rob.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא דַּעֲבִידָא לְאַגְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second way to split the cases instead of the one in Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A second split of the cases, based on the user's intention
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe the only way to settle them is by the kind of ship (Step 14).
steps.terutzMaskana: Even with a ship usually rented out: if he meant to rent, he pays rent. If he meant to rob, he pays only the damage.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב and שמואל do not argue. Each one rules about a different situation.

steps.title: רב הונא explains 'cracked' and 'invalidated' in the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about a stolen coin that cracked. רב הונא explains that 'cracked' means really cracked, and 'invalidated' means the government cancelled the coin.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'If he stole a coin and it cracked...' רב הונא said: 'Cracked' means it really cracked. 'Invalidated' means the government took the coin out of use.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It quotes a line from the משנה about a stolen coin, and רב הונא explains what its words mean.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה treats a cracked coin as changed, so the thief pays its value from the time of the theft. A coin that was only 'invalidated' can be returned as it is. רב הונא says that even a coin the government cancelled counts only as 'invalidated', not as changed.

phrases.english: "He robbed a coin and it cracked [etc.]"
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה. The משנה goes on to say that if the coin was only invalidated, he may return it as it is.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
"Cracked" means actually cracked;
"Invalidated" means the government invalidated it.

steps.triggerLanguage: גָּזַל מַטְבֵּעַ וְנִסְדַּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה, unrelated to the ship case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'Cracked' means a real crack (a change). 'Invalidated' means cancelled by the government, and such a coin may be returned as it is.

steps.title: רב יהודה: government cancellation counts as cracked
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says a coin cancelled by the government is the same as a cracked one. 'Invalidated' in the משנה means a coin cancelled in one province that is still used in another.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: A coin the government cancelled is the same as a cracked coin. So what does 'invalidated' mean? A coin that this province cancelled, but that people still use in another province.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה disagrees with רב הונא and gives his own meaning for the word 'invalidated' in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב יהודה, full government cancellation leaves the coin worthless, so it counts as changed, like a crack. Only a coin that still works somewhere else is just 'invalidated' and can be handed back as it is.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How do we picture it?
Goes out, is still used (as money)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two opinions. For רב הונא, government cancellation is 'invalidated' (return it as is). For רב יהודה, government cancellation is like 'cracked' (pay the original value).

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda said:
Invalidated by the government too is the same as cracked.
Rather, what is the case of "invalidated"?
Where this province invalidated it,
but it is still used in another province.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר: פְּסָלַתּוּ מַלְכוּת נָמֵי הַיְינוּ נִסְדַּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second opinion that argues with רב הונא's explanation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Government cancellation counts as a change, like a crack. 'Invalidated' means cancelled in one province but still used in another.

steps.title: רב חסדא challenges רב הונא from rotten fruit and sour wine
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא asks רב הונא: rotten fruit and sour wine are just like a coin the government cancelled, yet the משנה says the thief pays their value from the time of the theft. So why should a cancelled coin be returned as it is?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said to רב הונא: You say 'invalidated' means cancelled by the government. But look at fruit that rotted and wine that turned sour. They are like a coin the government cancelled, and the משנה teaches that the thief pays what they were worth when he stole them!
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא attacks רב הונא's explanation by pointing to other cases in the same משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rotten fruit and sour wine still exist but have lost their use, just like a coin the government cancelled. The משנה treats them as changed, so the thief must pay. That seems to contradict רב הונא, who lets the thief return a cancelled coin as it is.

keyTerms.meaning: As at the time of the robbery

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב חִסְדָּא לְרַב הוּנָא:
phrases.english: Rav Chisda said to Rav Huna:
According to you, who said
"invalidated" means invalidated by the government;
look at fruit that rotted,
wine that turned sour,
which are like something invalidated by the government;
and it teaches: he pays as at the time of the robbery!
phrases.notes: 'It teaches' points to our משנה, which lists these cases.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב חִסְדָּא לְרַב הוּנָא: לְדִידָךְ דְּאָמְרַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's explanation from Step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's claim that a coin cancelled by the government is only 'invalidated' and can be returned as is
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Rotten fruit and sour wine are like a cancelled coin, since the item still exists but has lost its use. The משנה makes the thief pay for them as they were at the time of the theft. So a cancelled coin should be treated the same way.

steps.title: רב הונא answers that the fruit and wine changed but the coin did not
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא answers רב חסדא. The rotten fruit and sour wine changed in taste and smell. A cancelled coin itself did not change at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: He (רב הונא) said to him: There, with the fruit and the wine, the taste and the smell changed. Here, with the cancelled coin, nothing about the coin changed.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא defends his view against רב חסדא's question from Step 18. He shows that a cancelled coin is different from rotten fruit and sour wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא said a cancelled coin is like spoiled fruit, so the thief should pay what it was worth when he stole it. רב הונא says no. The fruit and wine really changed in themselves, so they count as different objects. The coin is exactly the same coin, so the thief can return it as it is.

keyTerms.meaning: There / here (the other case versus this case)

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רב הונא answering רב חסדא's question from the step before.

phrases.english: There, its taste and its smell changed;
here, it did not change.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָתָם נִשְׁתַּנָּה טַעְמוֹ וְרֵיחוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of רב חסדא in Step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (חילוק): a physical change versus no physical change.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A cancelled coin seemed to be just like rotten fruit or sour wine, since all of them lost their value.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a real change in the object itself means the thief must pay the value from the time of the theft. A coin that did not change can be returned as it is.

steps.title: רבא challenges רב יהודה from impure תרומה
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks רב יהודה a question. Stolen תרומה that became impure is like a cancelled coin, yet the משנה says the thief may return it as it is. So why does רב יהודה treat a cancelled coin like a cracked one?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רב יהודה: You said a coin cancelled by the government is the same as a cracked coin. But look at stolen תרומה that became impure. That is just like a coin the government cancelled, and still the משנה teaches that the thief says to the owner: "Here is yours in front of you."
steps.whatsHappening: Now the challenge goes the other way. רבא attacks רב יהודה's view from Step 17, which said a cancelled coin is like a cracked one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Impure תרומה looks exactly the same, but nobody may eat it anymore. That is just like a coin that looks fine but the government no longer accepts. The משנה lets the thief return the impure תרומה as it is. So it seems a cancelled coin should also be returned as it is, which goes against רב יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: The government cancelled it (the coin is no longer legal money)
The portion of produce given to a כהן, which may only be eaten when it is pure
Here is yours in front of you (the thief returns the item as it is)

phrases.english: Rava said to Rav Yehuda:
According to you, who said
that a coin the government cancelled is also the same as "cracked";
but there is the case of תרומה that became impure,
which is like a coin the government cancelled,
and yet it teaches: he says to him,
"Here is yours in front of you"!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַב יְהוּדָה: לְדִידָךְ דְּאָמְרַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רב הונא's view was defended, the גמרא now challenges the opposite view of רב יהודה from Step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's view that a coin cancelled by the government is like a cracked coin, so the thief pays its value from the time of the theft.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Impure תרומה is the same kind of case: nothing looks different, but it is now useless. The משנה lets the thief return it as it is, so a cancelled coin should be treated the same way.

steps.title: רב יהודה answers that the coin's damage can be seen but the תרומה's cannot
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה answers that you cannot see the damage in impure תרומה. You can see the damage in a cancelled coin, because anyone can tell it is the cancelled type.
steps.simpleTranslation: He (רב יהודה) said to him: There, with the תרומה, the damage cannot be seen. Here, with the coin, the damage can be seen.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה defends his view by showing a difference between impure תרומה and a cancelled coin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Impure תרומה looks exactly like pure תרומה, so its loss is hidden and does not count as a visible change. A cancelled coin can be recognized just by looking at it, so its loss is out in the open. That makes it like a cracked coin, and the thief must pay its value from the time he stole it.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רב יהודה answering רבא.

phrases.english: There, its damage is not noticeable;
here, its damage is noticeable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָתָם לָא מִינְּכַר הֶיזֵּיקַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's קשיא in Step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (חילוק): damage you can see versus damage you cannot see.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Impure תרומה and a cancelled coin seemed alike, because both look the same as before but lost their value.
steps.terutzMaskana: Damage you can see, like a cancelled coin, counts like a real change, so the thief pays the value from the time of the theft. Hidden damage, like impure תרומה, lets the thief return the item as it is.
steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא: a cancelled coin is returned as it is, because the coin itself did not change, unlike rotten fruit. רב יהודה: a cancelled coin is like a cracked coin, because its damage can be seen, unlike impure תרומה.

steps.title: A new dispute about a loan in a coin that was later cancelled
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new dispute. Someone lent money to be repaid in a certain coin, and then that coin was cancelled. The text begins to quote רב's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: If someone lends money to his friend to be repaid in a certain coin, and that coin is cancelled, רב said:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new discussion about loans, not theft. It describes the case and starts to quote רב. His ruling comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the topic was a thief who stole a coin that was later cancelled. Now the question is about a lender and a borrower who agreed on a specific coin, and that coin stopped being legal money. The word אִיתְּמַר tells us that אמוראים disagree here, and רב's opinion is about to be given.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (opens a disagreement between אמוראים)
On the condition of a certain coin (to be repaid in that coin)

phrases.english: It was stated:
One who lends to his friend on a certain coin,
and the coin became cancelled,
Rav said:
phrases.notes: רב's actual ruling comes on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר: הַמַּלְוֶה אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ עַל הַמַּטְבֵּעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the theft case of a cancelled coin to a related case of a loan in a coin that was cancelled.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case of a loan to be repaid in a specific coin that was later cancelled. רב's ruling follows on the next amud.
